25-black-women-who-lost-federal-jobs-eco.headline: 25 Black Women Who Lost Federal Jobs - Economic Harm & Accountability
25-black-women-who-lost-federal-jobs-eco.author: Angela Bruce-Raeburn, MPA, M.A., MACSP.
25-black-women-who-lost-federal-jobs-eco.core: Posted in last 7 days 25 Black Women Who Lost Federal Jobs - Economic Harm & Accountability THE EXTRAORDINARY POWER OF BLACK WOMEN. AND THE PRICE WE KEEP PAYING. Once again, elections have reminded America of the extraordinary political power of Black women. We organize. We show up. We help shape the future of this country. But who shows up for us when our own lives are being dismantled? What has happened to Black women whose careers, livelihoods, and economic security have been decimated by the Trump administration. I am one of them. We did everything right. In fact, we did everything white supremacy demanded of us. We got the degrees. Often more than one. We worked twice as hard. We mastered the institutions that questioned our belonging. We built distinguished careers, served our country, raised families, bought homes, and saved for retirement. We believed that excellence, competence, and decades of service would mean something. We were wrong. The jobs disappeared. Careers built over decades were dismantled. Financial security evaporated. And the country moved on to the next headline. But we are still here. Still unemployed. Still watching savings disappear. Still wondering how we will pay our mortgages, protect our families, and rebuild futures that took a lifetime to secure. And please, do not call us resilient. Resilience has become the language America uses to congratulate Black women for surviving what it refuses to prevent. I am launching The Women Who Did Everything Right, beginning with a pilot of 25 Black women whose careers and livelihoods were disrupted by the actions against the federal workforce, including women working for federal contractors and affected organizations. I want to know where we are now. What we have lost. What this has cost our families. What it means to confront unemployment, financial insecurity, and professional erasure after decades of achievement. And I want to ask the questions that aren't being asked loudly enough. Where are the lawyers? Where are the employers? Where are the institutions that benefited from our labor? Who is documenting the damage? Who is fighting for restitution? Who is going to make us whole? This is not a project about celebrating our strength. It is about documenting the consequences of institutional decisions and demanding accountability, economic justice, and repair. I am looking for 25 Black women willing to begin this conversation with me. If you lost your federal job, were pushed out of public service, or worked for a federal contractor or organization affected by these decisions, please send me a private message. You do not have to share your story publicly. I also want to hear from attorneys, employers, recruiters, researchers, and organizations prepared to turn these stories into action. Black women have demonstrated, election after election, what we can do for this country. Now I want to know what this country is prepared to do for us. We are done being told to survive what should never have happened. We are demanding to be made whole.

uninsured-americans-managing-chronic-con.core: Posted in last 7 days Uninsured Americans - Managing Chronic Conditions Without Insurance I'm starting something new, and I need your help. 34 million Americans will be uninsured by 2027. Some lost coverage with a job. Some got priced out. Some decided a $450/month Bronze plan with a $10,000 deductible wasn't worth what they were paying. But these people will still get sick and still have chronic conditions they are managing. → People still get sick. So how are you doing it? That’s what I want to know. I'm launching a podcast (of sorts) where I sit down with people living without health insurance to talk about how they've made it work. Is it: - Cash-pay clinics and direct primary care - Concierge doctors - Health sharing ministries and telehealth - Community health centers and negotiating bills - Going overseas for care, or figuring it out as you go I want to hear your stories of what has worked, what hasn’t and what you wish someone had told you sooner. If this is you, or someone you know, I'd love to talk. Come on the show, or if you'd rather stay off mic, just tell me what you're doing now for care. Your experience could become an actual plan for someone who really needs one. Comment below or send me a message, and please share this with anyone you think has a story to tell.

I write for The Follow Up, a newsletter for over 40,000 B2B sales professionals. I’m looking to interview people in tech and software, especially SaaS, cybersecurity, AI, cloud, and data, about a real customer deal that taught them something. How did you start the conversation? marketing-communications-professionals-7.headline: Marketing Communications Professionals 7+ Years - Onboarding Series
marketing-communications-professionals-7.author: Faith Enang
marketing-communications-professionals-7.core: Posted in last 7 days Marketing Communications Professionals 7+ Years - Onboarding Series Over a year ago, a group of friends and colleagues came together to build what we now know as the97thstreet, a community for young Gen Z professionals and aspiring professionals in marketing communications. In the past year, we've grown into a little corner of the internet where we share conversations about the marketing industry, job opportunities, interesting campaigns, articles worth reading, brands doing exciting things and, well, brands that could probably do better. 😂 To celebrate our first anniversary, we wanted to do something a little different. Beyond sharing what's happening in the industry, we wanted to start telling the stories of the people who are actually making things happen in it. And that's how Onboarding by the97thStreet was born. The idea is simple: to give young and aspiring marketing communications professionals a closer look at what it takes to build a career in the industry, through honest conversations with people who have been doing the work. We want to show them the possibilities, the unexpected turns, the difficult decisions and everything in between. Hopefully, these conversations will help someone feel a little less alone as they figure out their own career journey. Last Friday, we published our first edition, featuring Fikayo Jegede. Fikayo got into marketing by accident. She initially wanted to become an OAP, but her career eventually took her in a different direction. Today, she's doing remarkable work in the industry and has even authored a book, 'Feex Your Marketing'. I particularly enjoyed this conversation because it reminded me of something many of us who studied Mass Communication eventually discover: our career journeys don't always follow the paths we imagined when we were in school. And that's perfectly fine. On a personal note, Onboarding is a project I'm particularly excited about because it allows me do two things I genuinely enjoy: journalism and my work in marketing communications. It gives me the opportunity to keep interviewing people, asking questions and telling stories while learning more about an industry I'm actively building my career in. In many ways, it's a meeting point for several of my interests and aspirations. Our first edition is out, and the second is coming next week. 🥳 I'll drop the link to the first interview in the comments. Please read it and let us know what you think! Also, I'm looking to speak with marketing communications professionals who have spent at least seven years in the industry. If that's you, or you know someone whose career journey would make for an interesting conversation, please indicate in the comments or tag them below. I'd love to get in touch. Here's to more stories, more conversations and more people finding their way in marketing communications! #ShowUp #WorkHard #Repeat
